frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power through pipeline and LNG exports, while European buyers seek alternative suppliers and more flexible contracts. Investment needs in upstream capacity create pressure for selective foreign participation.

frictionVectors.title: Morocco and Sahel tensions
frictionVectors.details: Rivalry with Morocco and instability across the Sahel complicate regional connectivity, border security, and energy diplomacy. Algiers remains wary of external military and political involvement near its southern borders.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to state revenue and export earnings, leaving Angola exposed to price volatility and declining mature-field output. International operators retain substantial influence over technology, capital, and offshore production.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: The rail corridor linking Angola to copper and cobalt regions is attracting US, European, and Chinese interest. Competing infrastructure and mineral-access agendas could strengthen Angola's leverage but also limit its strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and transit disputes
frictionVectors.details: Political relations with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and constrained the use of Benin's port as a regional outlet. External mediation and changing sanctions dynamics continue to shape reopening prospects.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel threatens northern communities, transport corridors, and investment confidence. Benin is expanding security cooperation with regional and Western partners while trying to preserve control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value and greater national control over marketing and beneficiation. The dispute tests the durability of its partnership with De Beers amid weaker global diamond demand.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and other mineral prospects attract foreign capital, but Botswana lacks the scale and processing capacity to control downstream value chains. Infrastructure and water constraints may increase reliance on external developers.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production, licensing, and marketing, challenging established foreign operators and informal supply networks. This may increase fiscal capture but risks deterring investment and encouraging smuggling.

frictionVectors.title: Security partnership realignment
frictionVectors.details: Burkina Faso has reduced reliance on French security ties and deepened cooperation with Russia-linked actors. The shift offers regime protection but increases geopolitical exposure, while persistent insurgency threatens mining zones and transport infrastructure.

highlights: Regional trade access is gradually improving

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold and nickel development attract foreign capital, but weak traceability and limited domestic processing constrain Burundi's control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions around eastern DRC and border security raise transport and trade risks, while Burundi remains dependent on regional corridors and external logistics.

highlights: Atlantic logistics are gaining strategic value
Stable institutions protect national bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dependence in ports and energy
frictionVectors.details: International investment supports port, airport, and renewable-energy infrastructure, but financing and operating partnerships can limit long-term policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime surveillance gap
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's large maritime zone remains difficult to police, leaving fisheries, transshipment, and narcotics routes vulnerable to external exploitation.

highlights: Oil and mining remain externally financed
Infrastructure corridors are strategic pressure points

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector rent concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, and emerging mining projects provide state revenue but remain vulnerable to opaque contracting, foreign operators, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport and agricultural production, while dependence on major road, rail, and pipeline corridors increases exposure to outside financiers.

highlights: Security partnerships substitute for state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security support has strengthened regime protection but deepened concerns that gold and diamond access is exchanged for security services outside transparent state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Weak control of mining zones
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, foreign traders, and porous borders constrain formal taxation and certification, preventing the government from capturing the full value of its mineral resources.

highlights: Security realignment is reshaping external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's budget and external bargaining power remain tied to petroleum exports, while pipeline and operating arrangements leave the state exposed to foreign technical and financial control.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan war and foreign basing pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict strains border security and humanitarian capacity, while shifting relations with France, Russia, and other partners complicate control over strategic military infrastructure.

highlights: Remittances and external aid anchor the economy

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' territorial sovereignty and sustaining a major diplomatic grievance. Maritime boundaries, migration, and access to surrounding waters remain contentious.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and infrastructure gaps
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, foreign assistance, and externally financed infrastructure. This narrows policy autonomy while weak transport and energy systems constrain domestic resource mobilization.

highlights: Critical minerals remain exposed to foreign leverage

frictionVectors.title: Eastern armed conflict
frictionVectors.details: The M23 conflict and wider armed-group violence continue to weaken Kinshasa's control in the east, with Rwanda and other regional actors accused of shaping security and mineral flows. Diplomatic pressure has not yet produced durable territorial stabilization.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper dependency
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt processing and infrastructure, while Western and Gulf actors seek greater access to strategic minerals. Weak local refining and contract-enforcement capacity limit the state's ability to capture full value.

highlights: Oil revenue stabilizes the state but narrows diversification
Chinese infrastructure ties deepen external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export earnings remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and foreign technical operators. Limited downstream capacity reduces domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and other infrastructure have strengthened connectivity but also contributed to creditor and repayment pressures. The government retains political control, yet financing needs constrain strategic autonomy.

highlights: Diversification is strengthening domestic economic leverage
Abidjan is consolidating as a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance in strategic sectors
frictionVectors.details: International firms retain strong positions in cocoa, energy, telecommunications, and port services. Abidjan is improving regulation and processing capacity, but local ownership and value capture remain incomplete.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Burkina Faso and Mali continues to pressure northern borders and security spending. Expanded regional partnerships improve resilience but may increase reliance on external military and intelligence support.

highlights: Port geography delivers strategic bargaining power
Foreign bases and debt constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major United States, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other foreign military facilities, converting strategic geography into revenue but exposing the country to great-power rivalry. The government must balance competing security partners without losing policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure linked to Ethiopia and Chinese financing provides essential income and regional leverage, while debt exposure and contested commercial arrangements limit sovereign control. Ethiopia's access needs make the corridor economically vital but politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian operation of the GERD, viewing downstream water flows as a core sovereignty and national-security issue. Negotiations remain vulnerable to regional escalation.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions and Gulf investment provide vital liquidity but increase outside influence over major infrastructure, ports, and state-linked assets. Cairo is balancing urgent financing needs against control of strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output is narrowing fiscal space and increasing dependence on foreign technical partners and offshore investment. The state retains formal control, but resource revenues and production capacity remain externally exposed.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea is seeking to preserve its LNG hub role amid competition from Nigeria, Cameroon, and emerging Gulf of Guinea projects. Limited reserves and aging infrastructure constrain its bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide crucial revenue but leave Eritrea dependent on foreign capital, expertise, and export channels. Sanctions exposure and opaque governance complicate long-term resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb draw competing attention from Gulf states and other external powers. Security partnerships could bring infrastructure benefits while narrowing Asmara's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, electricity, transport corridors, and customs revenues remain closely tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This dependence limits Mbabane's room to pursue fully independent economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and investment concentration
frictionVectors.details: Industrial parks, sugar, and textile production rely heavily on external markets and investors, especially through regional trade arrangements. Diversification is constrained by the small domestic market and political-risk perceptions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy and GERD tensions
frictionVectors.details: The GERD is expanding Ethiopia's leverage over electricity generation and national development, but its operation remains a major confrontation point with Egypt and Sudan. A durable basin-wide framework is still absent.

frictionVectors.title: Debt, conflict, and external infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and internal conflict constrain Addis Ababa's ability to finance infrastructure independently. Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners remain important, creating competing pressures over ports, telecoms, and strategic corridors.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese and other minerals, creating friction with established foreign operators and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains dependent on externally financed and operated transport infrastructure to move bulk commodities, limiting practical control over its resource corridors.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential security partner

frictionVectors.title: Cross-border sovereignty pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for security, trade access, and regional connectivity, producing persistent asymmetry in bilateral decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited enforcement capacity continue to threaten local livelihoods and weaken control over maritime resources.

highlights: Gold remains the core sovereign resource

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illicit and environmentally destructive mining, including activity involving foreign-linked networks, continues to erode state revenue and damage land and water resources.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local processing and strategic control over lithium and other minerals, but financing needs and external investment limit its negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore megaproject is attracting major foreign capital and infrastructure commitments, while rail, port, and revenue arrangements will determine how much value remains inside Guinea.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and investor risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining renegotiations to assert sovereignty, but political uncertainty and restrictions on civic space raise the risk of opaque deals and external leverage.

highlights: State capacity is weaker than elite competition

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign buyers and limited domestic processing leave producers vulnerable to price-setting outside the country and reduce sovereign control over the main export.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Weak oversight around Bissau’s port and maritime space creates openings for illicit trafficking and foreign influence, while regional security dependence remains substantial.

highlights: Port and energy assets remain strategic bargaining points

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: China, Gulf financiers, and multilateral lenders compete for influence over transport and energy projects. Fiscal pressure limits Nairobi's ability to dictate financing terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and Lamu remain exposed to regional competition and foreign-backed corridors. Control of customs, rail, and port revenues is politically sensitive.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on South Africa
Small economy exposed to external capital and markets

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue but structurally ties national infrastructure and water policy to South African demand and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Fiscal Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Manufacturing remains dependent on external trade preferences and foreign-owned supply chains. Any shift in US or regional market access can quickly reduce jobs and public revenue.

highlights: Mining revival attracts competing foreign interests
Infrastructure gaps limit domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and emerging mineral projects draw international investors while Liberia struggles to secure stronger local processing, tax, and employment benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and financiers remain important to port modernization and mineral transport. Weak infrastructure increases Liberia's dependence on concession-linked logistics.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided among rival power centers
Foreign security patrons shape critical infrastructure

frictionVectors.title: Oil Governance Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Competing institutions and armed networks contest control over production, export terminals, and revenue distribution. Shutdown threats continue to make national resource policy highly vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: External states and contractors retain leverage through security partnerships, arms support, and energy deals. This constrains unified Libyan control of oil infrastructure and border corridors.

highlights: Critical minerals drive investment without full value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented models. Madagascar faces persistent pressure to trade fiscal and environmental concessions for investment.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit Resource Networks
frictionVectors.details: Illegal rosewood, gold, and gemstone flows undermine state authority and conservation enforcement. Foreign buyers and intermediaries often capture more value than local communities or public institutions.

frictionVectors.title: IMF Austerity and External Financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms remain central to fiscal survival, narrowing Malawi's room to set independent subsidy, exchange-rate, and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects, including rare-earth and uranium interests, offer urgently needed revenue but expose the state to contract, environmental, and local-benefit disputes.

highlights: Gold and security partnerships remain contested

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bamako's reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western leverage but increases dependence on a powerful external partner and complicates access to transparent security and mining arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Control and Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking a larger share of gold value and tighter control over operators, while jihadist violence and contested territorial access undermine production, transport, and investor confidence.

highlights: Gas production opens a new bargaining phase

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and foreign operators expands fiscal potential, but cross-border governance, local-content expectations, and revenue transparency remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports depend heavily on external capital, rail infrastructure, and global commodity demand, leaving Mauritania exposed to price shocks and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement and Base Access
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty and future basing arrangements around the Chagos Archipelago remain a major test of Mauritius's ability to convert legal claims into effective strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Blue Economy
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius benefits from diversified investment, tourism, and financial links, but dependence on foreign capital and shipping routes limits autonomy in maritime infrastructure and ocean-resource development.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables support strategic leverage
Western Sahara remains the core sovereignty dispute

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses infrastructure, fisheries, phosphates, and renewable projects in the territory to reinforce its sovereignty claim, while Algeria and the Polisario Front reject that framework.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Technology and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and other partners are important to ports, rail, defense, and renewable-energy buildout; managing these relationships without excessive dependence is a continuing strategic challenge.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Foreign energy consortia and security partners remain central to protecting offshore gas and restarting delayed projects. Insurgency and dependence on external military support constrain Maputo's control over the resource corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional and overseas investors are competing for influence over the Nacala, Beira, and Maputo transport systems. Debt, concession terms, and cross-border mineral flows complicate sovereign infrastructure control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Minerals
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate much of Namibia's uranium, lithium, and emerging critical-minerals investment. Windhoek is seeking greater local processing and state participation without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Financing
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign finance, technology, and export demand, creating long-term exposure to outside partners. The government is attempting to retain more value through domestic infrastructure and industrial linkages.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are pressing foreign mining operators for revised terms and greater national control over uranium and other minerals. Political rupture with former Western partners raises operational and financing risks.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The crude-export route through Benin remains exposed to diplomatic conflict, border restrictions, and militant disruption. Niger's landlocked position leaves strategic infrastructure dependent on neighboring states and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Dependence and Contract Power
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain important for capital, technology, and offshore production, while crude theft and contract disputes erode state capture of value. Reforms are improving commercial discipline but have not eliminated external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Power Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment is needed to expand gas processing, pipelines, and electricity generation, leaving strategic infrastructure vulnerable to financing conditions and security failures. Local-content policies have increased participation but not yet closed the technology gap.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Traceability
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is expanding formalization and processing around tin, tantalum, and tungsten, but international scrutiny persists over mineral flows linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Export-market access depends increasingly on credible provenance controls.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security role in eastern Congo generates diplomatic pressure and sanctions risk while protecting its regional influence and commercial networks. External partnerships provide capability but constrain Kigali's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: EEZ Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Commercially viable offshore hydrocarbons remain unproven, leaving the country vulnerable to foreign negotiating leverage over future blocks and maritime data.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on outside finance, particularly from European and Chinese-linked partners, limiting domestic policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater state participation and transparency in oil, gas, and mining projects, creating tension with established foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and declining coastal stocks remain politically sensitive, with domestic fleets demanding stronger control over Senegalese waters.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Tuna Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains regulatory authority over its waters, but dependence on foreign industrial fleets and fishing revenues complicates enforcement and conservation.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, French, European, and Chinese engagement supports maritime surveillance and infrastructure while creating pressure to preserve strategic nonalignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, diamonds, and other minerals remain central to state revenues, but foreign operators retain substantial influence over capital, technology, logistics, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors and port infrastructure tie resource exports to external investors and lenders, limiting Freetown's ability to capture full downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Licensing Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Federal and member-state disagreements over offshore blocks create openings for foreign companies and political patrons to negotiate around incomplete national consensus.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors provide security and port-related support, but their competing interests can constrain unified Somali control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and logistics sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity, rail and port constraints weaken South Africa's ability to process and export minerals on its own terms. Private-sector concessions and foreign investment are increasingly necessary to restore capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China and Gulf actors are competing for influence over platinum-group metals, manganese and battery minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while avoiding alignment with any single external bloc.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports remain dependent on infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, exposing revenues and production to sabotage, outages and bargaining by external transit authorities.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector control and patronage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and trading intermediaries retain major influence over production, financing and marketing, while weak institutions limit transparent national control of petroleum revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of export corridors
frictionVectors.details: The SAF-RSF war has disrupted oil transit, gold production and trade routes, with armed actors and foreign sponsors competing for ports, mines and customs revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External access to gold and ports
frictionVectors.details: Regional powers and commercial networks remain deeply involved in Sudanese gold flows and Red Sea infrastructure. This externalization reduces civilian bargaining power and encourages war-financing economies.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is advancing long-delayed offshore LNG development while pressing investors for stronger domestic benefits, fiscal returns and local participation. Project financing and contract terms remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and railway competition
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam corridor is attracting Gulf, Chinese and Western-linked infrastructure interest as Tanzania positions itself against rival East African routes. Dependence on external finance could constrain strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's deep-water port and regional transit economy rely heavily on foreign shipping, logistics and construction capital. Competition among Chinese, Turkish, Gulf and European interests gives outside actors leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector modernization
frictionVectors.details: Togo is seeking investment and technical capacity to revive phosphate output and move toward local processing. The trade-off is between rapid external financing and preserving national control over a core export resource.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and cooperation are closely tied to Tunisia's management of irregular migration. This increases external influence over domestic security and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and reliance on imported gas constrain fiscal autonomy. Delays in renewable-energy investment and infrastructure financing add to vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and Oil Financing
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil corridor is strengthening export potential but remains exposed to foreign financing, environmental pressure, and sanctions-related scrutiny. The project could generate revenue while limiting policy flexibility during its capital-intensive phase.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's trade depends heavily on Kenyan and Tanzanian corridors, while regional security operations consume resources. Disruptions in the Great Lakes or Sudan-linked routes could raise costs and reduce bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt are attracting intensified competition from Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors. Zambia is seeking more local processing and fiscal value, but capital and technology dependence remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Rail Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and inadequate rail capacity constrain mineral expansion and export diversification. Reliance on regional corridors leaves Zambia exposed to transport disruptions and neighboring states' infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Ownership and Beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, gold, and other minerals attract foreign capital while Zimbabwe struggles to enforce local processing and transparent revenue capture. Export restrictions have increased state leverage but have not eliminated dependence on external markets and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, constrained access to international finance, and currency instability weaken domestic control over strategic projects. Infrastructure gaps force mining companies to rely on private or externally financed solutions.
